content: It’s been a while, happy Monday. This is the Monday Letter for June 8th, 2026. --- Physical Media Still Rocks My move to San Francisco was a bit of a whirlwind. I was lucky enough to get connected with my now-roommates (who are now some of my best friends) before the move, and they ended up securing our place. Only now do I appreciate what a gift that was, getting spared the gauntlet that is the San Francisco housing market. My only preview of our home was a brief Messenger video call where I could make out a few pixels of our space. I didn’t know the neighborhood at all, nor the city, so I had no real sense of what I was walking into. Since then it’s been full of pleasant surprises. One of my favorites has been how quickly the library became part of my life here. I was always going to spend some amount of time at SFPL—my mom is a librarian, after all. title: Geno Is Score

content: Happy 4/20. Here’s your Monday Letter for April 20th, 2026. --- Geno Is Score I’ll start by saying something controversial: I like sports. You might think that is not controversial at all, but I’m not sure it’s safe to say in San Francisco. There’s a place called “Sports Basement” where you can, sure, buy hiking boots, but good luck finding a football (of any variety). I get visceral enjoyment, and real inspiration, from watching a bunch of sweaty dudes I’ve never met try to put an object into a target. I’ll never forget waking up at 7am Pacific to watch Lionel Messi take his final step and earn World Cup glory. Or the heartbreak of rolling out of bed at five in the morning to watch Team Canada get crushed in this year’s Winter Olympics. There’s nothing like sport. As a kid, the Edmonton Oilers (my hometown hockey team) were miserable. content: It’s April. Did you get pranked on the first? My friend did, by a Waymo. The car told its riders to start humming to help the vehicle “calibrate” before the ride could start. Ha. Ha. Here’s the Monday Letter for April 6th, 2026. --- Line Dancing Line dancing is one of the best new things I’ve been doing this year. Every Sunday night, I stroll down to Lower Haight to join friends at the aptly named Lower Haight Line Dancing ("LHLD" from here on out, because that’s a mouthful). From 6 to 10pm, a handful of instructors run a line dancing class out of their garage, and it’s an absolute blast. There’s a great crowd, the dances are a ton of fun, and the song choices are great too. As an Albertan, country bars and line dancing are a core part of the cultural makeup. In middle school, the go-to was always “Cadillac Ranch.” (I looked it up and the first result was a tutorial from the Calgary Stampede organizers, so yeah, Albertan.) description: In this post, I explore the need for a new approach in SaaS to unleash the full potential of AI agents, drawing parallels to autonomous driving and my recent adventures in New York City.
content: And… we’re back! I’ve had a busy last couple of weeks, with trips to Whistler and New York. Lots to talk about. This is the Monday Letter for March 30th, 2026 (and March 23rd and March 16th). --- Give the agents an Autobahn Issue tracking is dead. Or so says the CEO of the hottest issue tracking company. As someone who works at another sort of issue tracking company (really, an everything tracking company), I don’t fully agree, but there’s some truth to it. What I think is dead is the how, more than the what. The “what” is fine. A system of record is still critical. Teams that are extremely organized dramatically leapfrog unorganized teams in the agent-driven era we find ourselves in. There’s still a cold-start problem with agents (you can’t just tell Claude, “build a sustainable business; make no mistakes”… yet), so a clear backlog with well-defined tasks is beneficial. title: Slopes and Systems
description: Michael reflects on the importance of consistent practice in honing skills while sharing insights from his weekend skiing trip and current reading pursuits.
content: Hello from thirty-four thousand, nine hundred and ninety-one feet. I’m on a return flight from Vancouver to San Francisco, and it is four hours to midnight, so it’s probably time for a letter. --- Slopes I spent this past weekend in Whistler, BC. It felt great to be back in Canada, and I felt great on the skis this time around. I’m a fairly average skier: comfortable on all blues, most blacks, and in solid conditions, I’ll occasionally attempt a double-black. I had the chance to ski with some great skiers. They all had the background you’d expect: a childhood close to a mountain, parents who were bought in (both figuratively and literally), and a real commitment to the craft. The common thread was simple: lots of hours on the slopes. It was an inspiring reminder that to be good at a thing, you need to do the thing. I get tripped up by the “slope” of my practice. description: As I prepare to graduate and deliver my speech, I reflect on the transformative journey of my undergraduate years and the responsibility we hold to shape the future with purpose and ownership.
content: I need to start with a confession. I don’t actually have a degree yet. But in ten days, I finally will. I know—it’s strange. Haven’t I been working full-time in San Francisco for nearly a year? There's more to the story, of course. Nearly a year ago, I effectively graduated—completing my undergraduate coursework with a final edit to a machine learning survey paper on sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) (which is most certainly outdated by now). But why didn't I get my degree? It came down to timing. I was scheduled to walk the stage right when my Notion internship was set to begin. After much deliberation over managing both graduation and a move to San Francisco, I had to declare bankruptcy on my time. I decided to focus solely on the move and postpone graduation until the following year. Ideally, a financial institution could predict whether or not someone will default ahead of time, and prevent it from happening in the first place. While this is a daunting task—and one that requires sensitivity given the fact we are dealing with people's financial livelihoods—this is a situation where machine learning can be of use. title: CSV Upload Tool
description: Easily upload and match your CSV data with this practical tool designed for seamless integration into larger projects!
content: Upload and match CSV data. Simple, but practical! Check out the project for yourself, here. Background This project was made for Artesian software, to be used in a more large scale project. Usage A user can upload a CSV file with any data, and then can match their "headers" (the columns) to the one's anticipated by the app. With these pairings, the app then "reassigns" the user's data with the new headings and saves it to a SQLite database. Check out some screenshots below! How it's made The project was made using React, Flask, and SQLite. I used Bootstrap to style the components. Challenges I struggled a decent amount to get SQLAlchemy to accept JSON data. Turns out they have a column type specifically for JSON. Consider this your friendly reminder to read the docs carefully! Accomplishments I think the user experience is really smooth, and the app is visually quite appealing! Future It'd be great to implement drag and drop.

title: Vietnam
description: Eleven days north to south, from Hanoi and the Ha Giang loop down to Saigon.
content: Hanoi Ha Giang Cat Ba Ninh Binh Ho Chi Minh City Eleven days up and down Vietnam over the April break on exchange. It ran north to south, from Hanoi out to the mountains and then down to Saigon. Hanoi came first: a free walking tour of the Old Quarter, egg coffee, Train Street, and the (muggy) views from the Lotte observation deck. Then the big one, the Ha Giang loop, a few days riding the mountain roads up near the Chinese border. After that an overnight bus to Cat Ba for a boat cruise with Cat Ba Ventures, the most chill day of the trip, and a stop in Ninh Binh for another boat through Trang An plus the Mua Caves in the fog. I flew down to Ho Chi Minh City to finish: Pizza 4P's, the War Remnants Museum, the Bitexco sky deck, a night on Bui Vien, and the Cu Chi tunnels the next morning, before flying home to Singapore. Route - Hanoi (Apr 7–9) - Ha Giang loop (Apr 10–12) - Cat Ba (Apr 13) - Ninh Binh (Apr 14) - Ho Chi Minh City (Apr 15–16) Where I stayed - Hanoi: Hanoi House, then Hanoi Backpackers - Ninh Binh: Green Mountain Homesta

title: Hong Kong
description: Six days of sightseeing wedged between paper deadlines on exchange.
content: Hong Kong Island Kowloon Lantau Island Six days in Hong Kong over the April break on exchange, mostly working on a paper between sightseeing, with a friend showing me around for part of it. I was based on Hong Kong Island at Check Inn: Causeway Bay, the Monster Building and the Quarry Bay promenade, the Central-Mid-Levels escalators, and a fair bit of laptop time in cafes and British pubs. One day I spent with my friend Jacky, ending at the horse racing. Over in Kowloon there was the waterfront and the Symphony of Lights. The best day was out on Lantau: the Ngong Ping 360 cable car up to the Tian Tan Buddha and the Wisdom Path, then the old fishing village at Tai O. I flew out late on the last night, landing in Hanoi around 1am to start the next trip. Route - Hong Kong Island (Apr 3–4) - Kowloon (Apr 5) - Lantau Island (Apr 6) Where I stayed - Hong Kong Island: Check Inn

title: Philippines
description: A week of island-hopping and diving through the Visayas.
content: Cebu City Panglao Moalboal A week island-hopping the Philippines with a friend, over the March break on exchange. It was mostly built around diving in the Visayas. We flew into Cebu before dawn and dove around Mactan, then ferried over to Bohol for Chocolate Hills, tarsiers, and a couple of days diving off Panglao. The plan had been to stop in Oslob for the whale sharks on the way south, but the ferry broke down, so we skipped it and pushed on to Moalboal. That turned out fine: the sardine run just off the beach, and canyoneering at Kawasan Falls. From there it was back up to Cebu City for a 3am flight onward to Malaysia. Palawan and El Nido were on the original plan and didn't survive the final cut; saving those for another lifetime. Route - Cebu / Mactan (Mar 23) - Bohol / Panglao (Mar 24–26) - Moalboal (Mar 27–28) Where I stayed - Cebu: Cebu Backpacker's Hostel, by the pier

title: Thailand
description: Temples up in Bangkok, then islands down south; eight days over a break on exchange.
content: Bangkok Koh Samui Krabi Eight days through Thailand while I was on exchange in Singapore, with a couple of friends joining partway. It split cleanly into temples up north and islands down south. I started in Bangkok for the big sights: Wat Pho, the Grand Palace and Wat Arun, the Chatuchak weekend market, and a day trip out to the old ruins at Ayutthaya. Evenings went to Khao San Road. From there I took the overnight train down to Surat Thani and crossed to Koh Samui for a couple of slow beach days. The trip finished in Krabi, based in Ao Nang, with a day out to the Phi Phi islands before flying back to Singapore via Kuala Lumpur. Route - Bangkok (Feb 18–20) - Koh Samui (Feb 21–22) - Krabi / Ao Nang (Feb 23–25) Where I stayed - Bangkok: Revolution Hostel, near Asok - Koh Samui: P&T Hostel - Krabi: K-Bunk, in Ao Nang

title: Indonesia
description: A week of temples and volcanoes across Java and Bali, on not much sleep.
content: Yogyakarta Malang Mount Bromo Mount Ijen Bali A week across Java and Bali with a friend, over a reading break on exchange. The pitch was temples and volcanoes, and it delivered on both; not much sleep was involved. We started in Yogyakarta for the two big temples, Prambanan and Borobudur, then took an overnight train east to Malang to reach the Tumpak Sewu waterfall. From there it was the classic East Java run: a pre-dawn jeep up Mount Bromo for sunrise over the caldera, then a midnight hike up Mount Ijen for the crater and its sulphur fires; we ran the Tumpak Sewu and Bromo legs with TrippyTrip Tour. We crossed by ferry to Bali to finish, with a day trip to Nusa Penida and sunset at Uluwatu before flying back to Singapore. It was rainy season the whole way and the early starts were brutal, but the volcanoes made it. Route - Yogyakarta (Feb 3–4) - Malang / Tumpak Sewu (Feb 5) - Mount Bromo (Feb 6) - Mount Ijen (Feb 7) - Bali (Feb 8–9) Where I stayed - Mount Bromo: Café Lava Hostel - Mount Ijen: Ijen Backpacker

title: Malaysia
description: Penang and the Cameron Highlands over a Chinese New Year weekend.
content: Penang Cameron Highlands Malaysia was the easy one to reach from Singapore, just over the causeway, so I ended up going a few times. This was the big loop, over the Chinese New Year long weekend in January. I crossed through Johor and took an overnight bus up to Penang. George Town is the draw: street art, hawker food in Little India, the Kek Lok Si temple, and a hike out to Monkey Beach in the national park. I caught the Chinese New Year fireworks there. From Penang I headed inland and up to the Cameron Highlands, where the afternoon went to a tea plantation above Tanah Rata. My notes for the back half of this trip never got written up, so I'll leave it there; Kuala Lumpur and Melaka were on the list and are worth their own visit. Route - Penang / George Town (Jan 21) - Cameron Highlands (Jan 22) Where I stayed - Cameron Highlands: Hiker's Sleep Port, in Tanah Rata
